CAPTOPRIL.clue: ACE inhibitor taken on an empty stomach; cough, high potassium, and airway swelling are reasons to stop and call
CAPTOPRIL.rationale: Captopril lowers blood pressure but can cause a dry cough, hyperkalemia, first-dose hypotension, and angioedema. ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and are stopped in pregnancy.

AMLODIPINE.clue: Calcium-channel blocker whose common bothersome effect is ankle swelling; do not stop blood-pressure medicine abruptly
AMLODIPINE.rationale: Amlodipine dilates arteries and can cause peripheral edema and flushing. Hold it and notify the provider if blood pressure is below the ordered limit.

AMIODARONE.clue: Antiarrhythmic that can scar the lungs and disturb the thyroid; report cough or dyspnea and avoid grapefruit
AMIODARONE.rationale: Amiodarone has a very long half-life and also affects the liver, skin, and corneas. It can raise digoxin and warfarin effect, so those doses often need review.

LIDOCAINE.clue: Drug for ventricular dysrhythmias whose toxicity looks neurologic: confusion, mouth numbness, and seizures
LIDOCAINE.rationale: Lidocaine is cleared by the liver, so heart failure and liver disease raise toxicity risk. As a local anesthetic, the form with epinephrine is not used on fingers, toes, the nose, ears, or penis.

ISOSORBIDE.clue: Long-acting nitrate for angina; headache is expected, and it must never be combined with an erectile-dysfunction drug
ISOSORBIDE.rationale: Isosorbide and nitroglycerin dilate veins and can drop blood pressure. Sit before rapid nitroglycerin, and allow a nitrate-free interval so tolerance does not develop.

SILDENAFIL.clue: Erectile-dysfunction drug that can cause a fatal blood-pressure drop if a nitrate is given
SILDENAFIL.rationale: Ask about sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil before every nitrate. Some of these drugs last more than a day, so a recent dose still counts.

CLOPIDOGREL.clue: Antiplatelet used after a coronary stent; do not stop it on your own, and expect it to be held before elective surgery
CLOPIDOGREL.rationale: Clopidogrel irreversibly inhibits platelets, so bleeding risk lasts for days. Sudden stopping soon after stent placement can thrombose the stent.

DABIGATRAN.clue: Oral thrombin inhibitor kept in its original bottle; do not open or crush the capsules because bleeding risk rises
DABIGATRAN.rationale: Dabigatran is sensitive to moisture, so it stays in the original container and the capsules are not opened. Idarucizumab reverses it, and it is not used with a mechanical heart valve.

BUBBLE.clue: Do not expel this from a prefilled enoxaparin syringe; inject into the abdomen and do not rub the site
BUBBLE.rationale: The air bubble in a prefilled enoxaparin syringe delivers the full dose and helps seal the track. Give it subcutaneously at 90 degrees, at least 2 inches from the umbilicus, and do not aspirate.

HIT.clue: Falling platelets plus new clots after heparin; stop every form of heparin, including flushes
HIT.rationale: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is a clotting emergency, not a bleeding disorder. Warfarin is not started alone while the platelet count is still low; a non-heparin anticoagulant is used instead.

HCTZ.clue: Thiazide diuretic abbreviation; it lowers potassium and can raise glucose, uric acid, and calcium
HCTZ.rationale: Hydrochlorothiazide is used for hypertension and mild fluid retention. Give it in the morning, watch for gout and hyperglycemia, and remember that thiazides raise lithium levels.

LABETALOL.clue: Alpha and beta blocker used for severe hypertension, including in pregnancy; watch heart rate and blood pressure
LABETALOL.rationale: Labetalol can cause bradycardia, bronchospasm, and a drop in blood pressure. The patient should stay lying down until the pressure is stable after an intravenous dose.

CLONIDINE.clue: Blood-pressure drug that can cause a dangerous rebound rise if it is stopped suddenly
CLONIDINE.rationale: Clonidine is a central alpha-2 agonist that also causes dry mouth and sedation. Taper it, and do not skip patch changes or oral doses.

PROPRANOLOL.clue: Nonselective beta blocker used for tremor and fast heart rate in hyperthyroidism; it can wheeze a patient with asthma
PROPRANOLOL.rationale: Propranolol blocks beta receptors in the lungs as well as the heart. Do not stop it abruptly, and remember that beta blockers hide the rapid heartbeat of low blood sugar.

MASK.clue: What a beta blocker does to the fast-heartbeat warning of low blood sugar; sweating may still occur
MASK.rationale: Patients with diabetes on a beta blocker can become hypoglycemic without tachycardia. Teach them to check glucose and to treat sweating, hunger, or confusion as possible low sugar.

ANGIOEDEMA.clue: Face, lip, or airway swelling from an ACE inhibitor; stop the drug and protect the airway
ANGIOEDEMA.rationale: Angioedema can progress to obstruction and is not the same as a dry cough. Do not give that ACE inhibitor again, and use epinephrine if breathing is threatened.

IBUPROFEN.clue: NSAID taken with food; it threatens kidneys and stomach and is avoided late in pregnancy
IBUPROFEN.rationale: Ibuprofen can cause bleeding, fluid retention, and kidney injury, especially with dehydration or other anti-inflammatories. Near term it can close the fetal ductus arteriosus.

KETOROLAC.clue: Potent injectable NSAID limited to a few days, typically no more than five; do not combine it with other NSAIDs
KETOROLAC.rationale: Ketorolac is for short-term pain and carries a high risk of bleeding and kidney injury. It is avoided in advanced kidney disease, active ulcers, and labor.

MEPERIDINE.clue: Opioid avoided in sickle cell disease and in older adults because a toxic metabolite can cause seizures
MEPERIDINE.rationale: Normeperidine accumulates, especially with kidney disease or repeated doses, and lowers the seizure threshold. Meperidine is also dangerous with MAOIs.

TRAMADOL.clue: Pain drug that lowers the seizure threshold and can trigger serotonin syndrome when combined with an SSRI
TRAMADOL.rationale: Tramadol has opioid effects, so it still depresses breathing, especially with other sedatives. A taper is safer than an abrupt stop after regular use.

PCA.clue: Pump that lets the patient dose opioid pain medicine; family members must not press the button
PCA.rationale: Only the patient uses patient-controlled analgesia, because a sleeping patient who is too sedated will not press it. Monitor sedation and respirations, since sedation comes before respiratory arrest.

SEDATION.clue: The warning that comes before opioid respiratory arrest; stimulate the patient and be ready to support breathing
SEDATION.rationale: Increasing drowsiness on an opioid means the next dose may stop breathing. Naloxone is titrated if depression occurs, and it can wear off before the opioid does.

SENNA.clue: Stimulant laxative scheduled with opioids, because a softener alone often does not produce a bowel movement
SENNA.rationale: Opioid constipation is expected and is prevented, not waited for. Fluids, fiber, and walking help, and the bowel regimen continues as long as the opioid does.

ALLOPURINOL.clue: Gout preventive that does not stop a flare already in progress; a new rash can be a severe reaction, so fluids are increased
ALLOPURINOL.rationale: Allopurinol lowers uric acid, is taken after meals, and is also used during tumor lysis. Stop it and report a rash, fever, or mouth sores.

COLCHICINE.clue: Acute-gout drug whose dose-limiting toxicity is diarrhea; stop it if diarrhea becomes severe
COLCHICINE.rationale: Colchicine is used for gout flares and can also cause bone-marrow suppression with longer use. It does not replace fluids or a preventive uric-acid plan.

FLUMAZENIL.clue: Benzodiazepine reversal drug that can precipitate seizures in a patient who takes those sedatives chronically
FLUMAZENIL.rationale: Airway support comes before flumazenil. Its effect is short, so sedation can return, and it is avoided in mixed overdoses that may include a tricyclic antidepressant.

LORAZEPAM.clue: Benzodiazepine used first for status epilepticus and for alcohol-withdrawal seizures; watch respirations
LORAZEPAM.rationale: Lorazepam stops seizures and treats alcohol withdrawal, but combined with opioids it can stop breathing. Do not stop long-term benzodiazepines abruptly.

NAC.clue: Abbreviation for the acetaminophen antidote, best when started early; the same drug is inhaled as a mucolytic
NAC.rationale: N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and limits liver injury after acetaminophen overdose. The usual adult ceiling for acetaminophen is 4 grams a day, and less if the liver is already harmed or alcohol use is heavy.

GLUCONATE.clue: Calcium salt that reverses magnesium toxicity and stabilizes the heart in severe hyperkalemia
GLUCONATE.rationale: Calcium gluconate is given slowly intravenously for magnesium toxicity and for dangerous hyperkalemia, where it protects the heart but does not remove potassium. Extravasation can damage tissue.

PPI.clue: Acid-suppressing drug class taken before breakfast; long-term use is linked to low magnesium, fractures, and C. difficile
PPI.rationale: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole are not instant antacids. Report black stools, and review any plan to stop one suddenly after an ulcer or a stent.

TSH.clue: Pituitary lab that is high in primary hypothyroidism and is used to adjust thyroid hormone replacement
TSH.rationale: A rising TSH usually means the levothyroxine dose is too low, if the problem is in the thyroid itself. Take the history of empty-stomach dosing before changing the dose.

PTU.clue: Antithyroid abbreviation preferred in the first trimester; watch for liver injury and a sudden sore throat
PTU.rationale: Propylthiouracil and methimazole can both cause agranulocytosis, so fever or pharyngitis means stop the drug and check the white count. After the first trimester, methimazole is usually preferred because propylthiouracil is harder on the liver.

STORM.clue: Life-threatening surge of thyroid hormone with high fever, tachycardia, and agitation after stress or surgery
STORM.rationale: Thyroid storm is cooled with a blanket and acetaminophen, slowed with a beta blocker, and blocked with an antithyroid drug. Aspirin is avoided because it can raise free hormone.

GRAVES.clue: Autoimmune cause of hyperthyroidism with bulging eyes, heat intolerance, and a rapid heart rate
GRAVES.rationale: Graves disease is treated with antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or surgery. Eye protection and a high-calorie diet matter while the metabolic rate is high.

TINGLING.clue: Early sign of low calcium around the mouth and in the fingers after thyroid or parathyroid surgery
TINGLING.rationale: Tingling, muscle spasm, and a positive Chvostek or Trousseau sign mean hypocalcemia from parathyroid injury. Keep calcium gluconate available and protect the airway if tetany starts.

HHS.clue: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state: extreme glucose and dehydration in type 2 diabetes, with little or no ketoacidosis
HHS.rationale: HHS patients are often older and neurologically impaired from dehydration. Fluids come first, then insulin, and glucose is not driven down faster than the brain can tolerate.

SICKDAY.clue: Illness plan in which insulin is continued even if the person is not eating, and glucose and ketones are checked more often
SICKDAY.rationale: Skipping insulin on a sick day is a common path to ketoacidosis. Sip sugar-containing fluids if food is not possible, and call for vomiting, large ketones, or rising glucose.

SOMOGYI.clue: Rebound morning high glucose caused by unrecognized nighttime hypoglycemia; check a 2 or 3 a.m. reading
SOMOGYI.rationale: If the middle-of-the-night glucose is low, the bedtime insulin may be too much or a snack is needed. This is the opposite of a dawn rise, which is high all night.

DAWN.clue: Early-morning high glucose from growth hormone and cortisol, without a low reading in the middle of the night
DAWN.rationale: The dawn phenomenon is managed by adjusting the evening insulin, not by assuming the patient went low. A 2 or 3 a.m. glucose tells it apart from rebound hyperglycemia.

REGULAR.clue: Short-acting insulin used for intravenous infusions; when mixing, draw it before NPH
REGULAR.rationale: Regular insulin is clear, peaks in about 2 to 3 hours, and is the insulin used intravenously. Inject air into NPH first, then into regular, draw regular, then draw NPH.

NPH.clue: Intermediate insulin abbreviation; it looks milky, is rolled not shaken, and is never given intravenously
NPH.rationale: NPH peaks roughly 4 to 12 hours later, so hypoglycemia can come in the afternoon or evening. It is not mixed with glargine or detemir.

GLUCOSE.clue: Fifteen grams of this fast carbohydrate are given to an awake patient with low blood sugar who can swallow, then the level is rechecked in 15 minutes
GLUCOSE.rationale: Juice, glucose tablets, or gel treat mild hypoglycemia. Recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still low, then give a longer-acting snack if the next meal is far off.

UNCONSCIOUS.clue: State in which nothing is given by mouth for low blood sugar; use intramuscular glucagon or intravenous dextrose
UNCONSCIOUS.rationale: Oral carbohydrate in an unresponsive patient causes aspiration. Glucagon can fail if liver glycogen is gone, as in starvation or heavy alcohol use, so intravenous dextrose is then required.

PEAK.clue: Time after an insulin dose when hypoglycemia is most likely; it is soon for lispro, a few hours for regular, and many hours for NPH
PEAK.rationale: Glargine and detemir have no pronounced peak. Schedule snacks and monitoring around the peak of the insulin that was given.

FOOTCARE.clue: Daily inspection, shoes indoors and out, and no heating pads for a patient with diabetic nerve damage
FOOTCARE.rationale: Neuropathy means a foot injury is not felt. Nails are cut straight, lotion is kept out from between the toes, and calluses are not self-trimmed.

INSIPIDUS.clue: ADH deficiency with huge volumes of dilute urine and rising sodium; do not fluid-restrict the way you would in SIADH
INSIPIDUS.rationale: Diabetes insipidus causes dehydration and hypernatremia. Desmopressin replaces the missing hormone, and too much of it causes water intoxication and a low sodium.

PIGMENT.clue: Skin darkening in primary adrenal failure, together with salt craving, low blood pressure, and high potassium
PIGMENT.rationale: Addison disease can cause shock if steroids are stopped or illness adds stress. Give intravenous glucocorticoid and fluid, and increase the steroid dose for surgery or fever.

SERTRALINE.clue: SSRI that can increase suicidal thinking in the first weeks and can cause serotonin syndrome if combined with an MAOI
SERTRALINE.rationale: Sertraline takes weeks to lift mood and can cause sexual dysfunction, nausea, and insomnia. Do not stop it abruptly, and avoid St. John's wort and tramadol.

BUPROPION.clue: Antidepressant also used to stop smoking; it is avoided in seizure disorders and eating disorders
BUPROPION.rationale: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is more activating than sedating, so it is not a bedtime drug. It has fewer sexual side effects than SSRIs.

BUSPIRONE.clue: Anti-anxiety drug that is not a benzodiazepine, takes weeks to work, and is not used as a rescue pill
BUSPIRONE.rationale: Buspirone does not sedate or cause dependence the way benzodiazepines do. Grapefruit juice raises its level, and it will not stop a panic attack that is happening now.

HALOPERIDOL.clue: High-potency typical antipsychotic that causes movement side effects, a malignant high-fever syndrome, and QT prolongation
HALOPERIDOL.rationale: Haloperidol is used for psychosis and acute agitation. Acute dystonia is treated with benztropine or diphenhydramine, and rigid high fever may be neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

OLANZAPINE.clue: Atypical antipsychotic with heavy weight gain, high glucose, and sedation; metabolic labs are part of follow-up
OLANZAPINE.rationale: Olanzapine is used in schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Antipsychotics raise death risk in dementia-related psychosis and are not a routine sedative for older adults.

PHENELZINE.clue: MAOI antidepressant that can cause a hypertensive crisis with aged cheese, cured meats, or an SSRI
PHENELZINE.rationale: Phenelzine requires a tyramine-restricted diet and a washout before other antidepressants. A sudden occipital headache and stiff neck are an emergency; phentolamine is the classic antidote.

WASHOUT.clue: Waiting period of about two weeks between an MAOI and an SSRI; fluoxetine needs about five weeks because it lasts so long
WASHOUT.rationale: Skipping the washout can cause serotonin syndrome. The same gap applies to meperidine and many other serotonergic drugs.

JOHNSWORT.clue: Herbal antidepressant that induces liver enzymes and can cause serotonin syndrome with an SSRI
JOHNSWORT.rationale: St. John's wort lowers levels of cyclosporine, oral contraceptives, warfarin, and some HIV drugs. Patients should tell every prescriber they are taking it.

NMS.clue: Malignant syndrome from antipsychotics: lead-pipe rigidity, very high fever, and unstable vital signs developing over days
NMS.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is treated by stopping the drug, cooling, hydrating, and often giving dantrolene or bromocriptine. It is slower and more rigid than serotonin syndrome.

EPS.clue: Movement effects of antipsychotics, including acute muscle spasm, restlessness, and parkinsonism
EPS.rationale: Extrapyramidal symptoms are more common with high-potency typical antipsychotics. Acute dystonia is an emergency if the airway is involved and is treated with benztropine or diphenhydramine.

DYSTONIA.clue: Sudden muscle spasm from an antipsychotic, including neck twisting or an eye crisis; laryngeal spasm can close the airway
DYSTONIA.rationale: Acute dystonia is reversed with intravenous diphenhydramine or benztropine. Stay with the patient until the airway is clearly safe.

SEROTONIN.clue: Syndrome of clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea, shivering, and fever from combining serotonergic drugs; onset is hours, not days
SEROTONIN.rationale: Serotonin syndrome is different from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which has lead-pipe rigidity and a slower onset. Stop the offending drugs, support vital signs, and use cyproheptadine when ordered.

CLONUS.clue: Rhythmic ankle beats when the foot is pushed up; in preeclampsia this warns that a seizure may be close
CLONUS.rationale: Clonus with hyperreflexia in a pregnant patient with hypertension is a severe feature. Keep the environment quiet, have suction and calcium gluconate ready, and do not leave the patient.

CIWA.clue: Scale that scores alcohol-withdrawal symptoms and guides benzodiazepine doses
CIWA.rationale: The Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment looks at tremor, sweating, anxiety, agitation, and vital signs. A rising score means more medication and closer monitoring, not a wait-and-see approach.

WERNICKE.clue: Receptive aphasia: speech is fluent but does not make sense, and the patient does not understand you
WERNICKE.rationale: Wernicke aphasia is a temporal-lobe injury. Use simple gestures and a calm manner, and do not rely on spoken teaching alone.

COARSE.clue: Large tremor, with vomiting or confusion, that means lithium toxicity rather than the expected fine tremor
COARSE.rationale: A fine tremor can be a side effect at a therapeutic lithium level of about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L. Dehydration, low sodium, thiazides, and NSAIDs push the level into the toxic range.

SUICIDE.clue: Ask about this directly, remove belts and cords, and use one-to-one observation when the risk is high; a contract is not enough
SUICIDE.rationale: Asking does not plant the idea. The danger is greatest with a plan, means, and intent, and also when energy returns in the first weeks of an antidepressant.

MANIA.clue: Elevated, sleepless, risky state in bipolar disorder; offer high-calorie finger foods and set consistent limits
MANIA.rationale: A manic patient will not sit for a meal and can become dehydrated. Reduce stimulation, do not argue grandiose ideas, and watch lithium levels if that drug is used.

REFEEDING.clue: Danger when nutrition restarts in a starved patient; the hallmark lab change is a falling phosphate
REFEEDING.rationale: Refeeding syndrome also drops potassium and magnesium and can cause edema and heart failure. Feed low and slow, and replace electrolytes before they bottom out.

BULIMIA.clue: Binge-purge illness, often at a normal weight, that causes low potassium, dental erosion, and enlarged salivary glands
BULIMIA.rationale: Vomiting produces metabolic alkalosis and a callused knuckle. Supervise after meals, watch the heart for potassium effects, and do not dismiss the illness because the weight looks normal.

ALCOHOL.clue: No safe amount in pregnancy; withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens, so use a benzodiazepine scale and give thiamine
ALCOHOL.rationale: Alcohol is teratogenic at any amount. In the hospital, thiamine comes before glucose, and a disulfiram-like reaction occurs if alcohol is taken with metronidazole.

OXYGEN.clue: A drug that supports combustion; no smoking or oil-based products near it, and the flow is shut off if a fire starts and the patient can be moved
OXYGEN.rationale: Oxygen is titrated to the ordered saturation, often about 88 to 92 percent in chronic carbon-dioxide retainers, and is never withheld from a hypoxic patient. Humidify higher cannula flows, and use water-based lubricant on the nares.

VENTURI.clue: Mask that delivers a precise oxygen percentage and is preferred when a patient with COPD needs a set concentration
VENTURI.rationale: A Venturi mask uses color-coded adapters for a known FiO2. It is a better choice than guessing with a nasal cannula when carbon-dioxide retention is a concern.

SILENT.clue: Chest with no wheeze in a severe asthma attack, which can mean no air is moving; this is worse, not better
SILENT.rationale: A silent chest, inability to speak, and falling oxygen mean impending respiratory failure. Give oxygen, a short-acting bronchodilator, and steroids, and prepare to ventilate.

CROUP.clue: Barking cough and inspiratory stridor from viral airway swelling; cool mist and a steroid help, and racemic epinephrine is for worse cases
CROUP.rationale: Croup is usually worse at night and shows a steeple sign if filmed. It is not epiglottitis: the child with croup can cough and is not typically drooling in a toxic tripod.

DROOLING.clue: Sign of epiglottitis in a child sitting forward; do not use a tongue blade, and do not leave the child
DROOLING.rationale: Epiglottitis can close the airway in minutes, so keep the child calm on a parent's lap and prepare for a controlled airway. The Hib vaccine prevents many cases.

MONTELUKAST.clue: Leukotriene blocker taken in the evening for asthma control; mood and suicidal thoughts are reported, and it does not stop an acute attack
MONTELUKAST.rationale: Montelukast is prevention, not rescue. Parents are taught to report behavior changes, nightmares, or depression.

TENDON.clue: Structure a fluoroquinolone can rupture; stop the drug and report calf or heel pain, and avoid this class in pregnancy and children
TENDON.rationale: Fluoroquinolones also prolong the QT interval and cause photosensitivity. Older adults and patients on steroids are at higher risk of tendon injury.

ETHAMBUTOL.clue: Tuberculosis drug that can inflame the optic nerve; report blurred vision or a change in color vision and stop the drug
ETHAMBUTOL.rationale: Ethambutol toxicity is detected with baseline and periodic eye exams. It is one of several TB drugs, and the liver is still watched because companion drugs injure it.

ORANGE.clue: Color that body fluids turn on rifampin; contact lenses can stain, and this is expected rather than bleeding
ORANGE.rationale: Rifampin also induces liver enzymes, so hormonal contraceptives fail and warfarin effect falls. Teach a backup birth-control method and watch for jaundice.

DOT.clue: Watching a patient swallow each tuberculosis dose so resistance does not develop
DOT.rationale: Directly observed therapy is a public-health tool, not a punishment. Incomplete treatment breeds multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, which is harder to cure and still requires airborne precautions.

TIDALING.clue: Rise and fall of the water-seal level with breathing; it stops when the lung has reexpanded or the tube is kinked
TIDALING.rationale: Tidaling in a chest-drainage system is expected while the lung is still down. Sudden stop plus respiratory distress suggests obstruction, not recovery, until breath sounds and the tubing are checked.

BUBBLING.clue: Continuous air movement in the water-seal chamber means a leak; gentle air movement in a wet suction-control chamber is expected
BUBBLING.rationale: Intermittent air in the water seal can occur while a pneumothorax is evacuating. New continuous air in that chamber means check the connections and the dressing before assuming the lung has worsened.

OCCLUSIVE.clue: If a chest tube pulls out of the chest, cover the site with a sterile dressing taped on three sides so air can escape
OCCLUSIVE.rationale: A fully sealed dressing over a fresh chest-tube site can trap air and cause tension pneumothorax. Stay with the patient, give oxygen, and call for a new tube.

HEMOTHORAX.clue: Blood in the pleural space; a sudden large volume of bloody chest-tube output with low blood pressure is reported immediately
HEMOTHORAX.rationale: Hemothorax is drained with a chest tube, and output is measured often. Clamping the tube to stop the drainage can cause tension and hidden blood loss.

OBTURATOR.clue: Guide kept at the bedside with a spare tracheostomy tube; it is used only to insert the tube and is then removed so air can pass
OBTURATOR.rationale: If a mature tracheostomy tube comes out, the obturator helps replace it. A fresh tract can close quickly, so call for help and do not force a false passage.

INFLUENZA.clue: Droplet-precaution illness with an annual vaccine; an egg allergy alone is not a reason to skip the vaccine, and antivirals work best within 48 hours
INFLUENZA.rationale: Influenza can lead to pneumonia and is especially dangerous in pregnancy, in older adults, and in chronic disease. The injectable vaccine is inactivated; the nasal vaccine is live.

PENICILLIN.clue: Antibiotic class that can cause anaphylaxis; observe after a first dose and do not leave a wheezing patient
PENICILLIN.rationale: A true penicillin allergy is hives, swelling, or breathing trouble, not simple nausea. Give it on an empty stomach when the product requires that, and teach the patient to finish every dose.

CLINDAMYCIN.clue: Antibiotic strongly linked to C. difficile; report watery diarrhea and do not take an antidiarrheal until that is ruled out
CLINDAMYCIN.rationale: Clindamycin colitis can start during treatment or weeks later. Stools are tested, and treatment is oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin, not intravenous vancomycin.

VARICELLA.clue: Chickenpox, which needs airborne and contact precautions until lesions crust; pregnant staff who are not immune do not enter
VARICELLA.rationale: Varicella is contagious before the rash and until every lesion is crusted. The vaccine is live and is not given in pregnancy, and shingles is the later reactivation.

MMR.clue: Live vaccine against measles, mumps, and rubella; do not give it in pregnancy, and avoid conceiving for about a month afterward
MMR.rationale: If a postpartum patient is not immune to rubella, give MMR before discharge. It is also withheld in severe immunosuppression.

LIVE.clue: Vaccine type, including MMR, varicella, and nasal influenza, that is contraindicated in pregnancy and in severe immunosuppression
LIVE.rationale: Inactivated vaccines such as the injectable flu shot and Tdap are given in pregnancy. A live vaccine is delayed until after birth.

NEEDLESTICK.clue: Wash with soap and water and report at once so HIV prophylaxis can start within hours; mucous membranes are flushed instead
NEEDLESTICK.rationale: Do not recap the needle. Occupational health tests the source when possible and starts post-exposure prophylaxis as soon as it is indicated, ideally within hours.

SPORES.clue: Form that lets C. difficile survive alcohol gel; use soap and water, and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin rather than the intravenous form
SPORES.rationale: Intravenous vancomycin does not reach the colon in useful amounts. Antidiarrheal drugs are avoided, and contact precautions continue per policy.

BLEACH.clue: Surface disinfectant that kills C. difficile spores; ordinary alcohol wipes do not
BLEACH.rationale: Rooms of patients with C. difficile are cleaned with a sporicidal product such as bleach. Hand washing with soap and water is required on the way out.

NEGATIVE.clue: Air-pressure room for tuberculosis, measles, and chickenpox; the door stays closed and staff wear a fitted respirator
NEGATIVE.rationale: Negative pressure keeps infectious droplet nuclei inside the room. A surgical mask on the staff member is not enough for airborne disease.

NEUTROPENIC.clue: Low neutrophil state in which fever is an emergency, rectal temperatures are avoided, and sick visitors stay out
NEUTROPENIC.rationale: A neutropenic patient may have infection with only a small temperature rise and no pus. Blood cultures and antibiotics are not delayed for a full workup if the patient is unstable.

PURPURA.clue: Purple nonblanching lesions with fever that mean meningococcemia until proved otherwise; start droplet precautions and antibiotics immediately
PURPURA.rationale: Meningococcal sepsis can kill within hours. Close contacts need prophylaxis, and a lumbar puncture must not delay antibiotics if the patient is unstable.

ISOTONIC.clue: Fluid that stays in the vessels, such as normal saline or lactated Ringer, used for volume loss and shock
ISOTONIC.rationale: Isotonic crystalloid expands intravascular volume. Only normal saline is run with blood, because lactated Ringer contains calcium and can clot the product.

OVERLOAD.clue: Crackles, neck-vein distention, and dyspnea from fluid given too fast; stop the infusion, raise the head, and notify the provider
OVERLOAD.rationale: Infants, older adults, and patients with heart or kidney failure overload easily. Daily weights and intake and output catch the problem before pulmonary edema.

HYPOKALEMIA.clue: Low potassium with muscle weakness, ileus, flat T waves, and U waves; it makes digoxin toxicity much more likely
HYPOKALEMIA.rationale: Loops, thiazides, vomiting, and diarrhea waste potassium. Replace it orally or by a slow pump infusion, never by IV push, and only if the patient is making urine.

PEAKED.clue: T-wave shape of dangerous hyperkalemia; stop potassium, protect the heart with calcium, and shift potassium with insulin plus dextrose
PEAKED.rationale: Peaked T waves can widen the QRS and stop the heart. Kidney failure, ACE inhibitors, and potassium-sparing diuretics are common causes.

LOWSODIUM.clue: Low sodium that causes confusion and seizures; restrict fluid in SIADH, and do not correct a chronic deficit too fast
LOWSODIUM.rationale: Severe hyponatremia is a seizure risk. Correcting chronic hyponatremia too quickly can cause osmotic demyelination.

VERIFY.clue: Two clinicians check the blood product, the patient identifiers, the type, and the expiration before it is hung
VERIFY.rationale: Most deadly transfusion reactions are clerical. Stay with the patient for the first 15 minutes, use only normal saline, and finish the unit within 4 hours.

TRANSFUSION.clue: Stop the blood at the first sign of a reaction, keep the vein open with new tubing and normal saline, and send the bag back to the lab
TRANSFUSION.rationale: Do not discard the product. Fever, back pain, dyspnea, hives, or a feeling of doom during a transfusion is a reaction until proved otherwise.

HEMOLYTIC.clue: Transfusion reaction from ABO incompatibility, with fever, back or flank pain, hypotension, and dark urine
HEMOLYTIC.rationale: A hemolytic reaction can cause shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Stop the blood immediately, support blood pressure, and do not restart that unit.

TACO.clue: Transfusion overload with dyspnea and high blood pressure; slow the rate, sit the patient up, and expect a diuretic
TACO.rationale: Transfusion-associated circulatory overload looks like heart failure. It differs from TRALI, which causes noncardiogenic lung edema with hypotension and fever.

TRALI.clue: Transfusion lung injury with acute dyspnea, fever, and low blood pressure, unlike volume overload which raises blood pressure
TRALI.rationale: TRALI is treated with oxygen and ventilatory support, not with aggressive diuresis as the first move. The blood bank is notified so the donor can be investigated.

CONSISTENT.clue: How vitamin K intake should stay on warfarin; a sudden binge of leafy greens drops the INR
CONSISTENT.rationale: Patients may eat greens, but the amount should not swing wildly. Report bleeding, keep follow-up INRs, and avoid adding aspirin or a new antibiotic without asking.

LACTATE.clue: Lab that rises when tissues are underperfused, as in sepsis and shock; a falling value suggests resuscitation is working
LACTATE.rationale: Lactate is a marker of hypoperfusion, not a diagnosis by itself. In sepsis, rapid crystalloid, often about 30 mL/kg when pressure is low or lactate is high, is given with antibiotics.

CARDIOGENIC.clue: Shock from pump failure, with crackles, cool skin, and a high filling pressure; extra fluid can drown the lungs
CARDIOGENIC.rationale: Cardiogenic shock needs inotropes and treatment of the cause, often a myocardial infarction, not a large fluid bolus. Blood pressure may be low while the lungs are overloaded.

NEUROGENIC.clue: Shock from lost sympathetic tone, with low blood pressure and a slow heart rate and warm dry skin
NEUROGENIC.rationale: Neurogenic shock differs from hypovolemic shock, which has a fast heart rate and cool clammy skin. It occurs with high spinal cord injury and is treated with fluids and vasopressors.

AFIB.clue: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no P waves; control the rate and anticoagulate to cut stroke risk unless the patient is unstable
AFIB.rationale: Unstable atrial fibrillation with hypotension or ischemia gets immediate synchronized cardioversion. If the rhythm has lasted more than about 48 hours, cardioversion can throw a clot unless anticoagulation or a clot check is done.

APICAL.clue: Pulse listened to for a full minute before digoxin; hold the dose if it is below the ordered rate, often 60 in adults and 90 in infants
APICAL.rationale: The apical impulse is normally at the fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line. Yellow halos, nausea, and bradycardia suggest digoxin toxicity, especially if potassium is low.

HALOS.clue: Yellow or green visual rings that suggest digoxin toxicity; hold the drug and check the level and the potassium
HALOS.rationale: Digoxin toxicity also causes anorexia, nausea, and slow or irregular rhythms. Low potassium, low magnesium, and kidney disease make it more likely.

SVT.clue: Very fast regular narrow-complex rhythm; adenosine is a rapid push, and a stable patient may try a vagal maneuver first
SVT.rationale: Supraventricular tachycardia is cardioverted if the patient is unstable. Adenosine is given fast with a flush and can cause a brief pause, so a monitor and crash cart are in the room.

DEFIB.clue: Unsynchronized shock for pulseless ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation; clear the bed before discharging
DEFIB.rationale: Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are not shockable. Resume compressions immediately after the shock, and remove medication patches first so the skin is not burned.

ASYSTOLE.clue: Flatline rhythm that is not shocked; confirm the leads, start compressions, and give epinephrine
ASYSTOLE.rationale: Asystole is treated like pulseless electrical activity: CPR, epinephrine, and a search for reversible causes. A fine ventricular fibrillation can look flat, so check a second lead.

PEA.clue: Organized rhythm on the monitor with no pulse; compress, give epinephrine, and look for causes such as hypovolemia, hypoxia, and tension pneumothorax
PEA.rationale: Pulseless electrical activity is not defibrillated. Hs and Ts include potassium problems, hydrogen ion, hypothermia, tamponade, thrombosis, and toxins.

PACING.clue: External pads for symptomatic bradycardia that does not respond to atropine, or for high-grade heart block; it hurts, so sedate if the patient is awake
PACING.rationale: Capture means each pacemaker spike is followed by a QRS and a pulse. Failure to capture means check connections and increase output as ordered while supporting the airway.

CHEWED.clue: How aspirin is taken in suspected acute coronary syndrome so it absorbs faster, unless there is a true allergy or another contraindication
CHEWED.rationale: Chewed aspirin inhibits platelets quickly. Oxygen is added for low saturation, not automatically for every chest-pain patient, and opening a blocked artery is the priority in ST-elevation infarction.

REPERFUSION.clue: Opening the blocked coronary artery, which is the priority in ST-elevation myocardial infarction rather than a fixed drug ritual
REPERFUSION.rationale: The cath lab is preferred when it can be reached promptly. Thrombolytics are considered when timely PCI is impossible and bleeding risk is acceptable, after a bleed has been judged unlikely.

MURMUR.clue: Sound of turbulent flow; a new one plus fever suggests endocarditis until proved otherwise
MURMUR.rationale: Endocarditis vegetations embolize to brain, kidney, spleen, or lung. Draw cultures before antibiotics, and reserve dental prophylaxis for the highest-risk hearts, such as a prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis.

PRELOAD.clue: Stretch on the heart at the end of filling; diuretics and venodilators such as nitroglycerin reduce it
PRELOAD.rationale: High preload causes congestion and edema. Low preload, as in bleeding, drops cardiac output and is treated with volume, not with more diuretic.

BNP.clue: Hormone lab that rises when the ventricles are stretched by heart failure and helps explain unexplained dyspnea
BNP.rationale: B-type natriuretic peptide is higher in decompensated heart failure and lower when the cause of dyspnea is purely lung disease. Kidney failure can also raise it.

JVD.clue: Neck-vein distention seen in fluid overload, right-sided heart failure, and cardiac tamponade
JVD.rationale: Jugular venous distention with crackles suggests the patient will not tolerate more fluid. With muffled sounds and hypotension it is part of tamponade.

BECK.clue: Triad of low blood pressure, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds in cardiac tamponade
BECK.rationale: Beck triad is a late, classic picture. After cardiac surgery, a sudden stop in chest-tube drainage plus this picture means clot is compressing the heart and needs immediate drainage.

VENOUS.clue: Insufficiency with brown lower-leg staining, edema, and wet ulcers near the medial ankle, eased by elevation
VENOUS.rationale: Compression stockings are applied in the morning before edema forms, but only if arterial pulses and the ankle-brachial index are adequate. A sudden one-leg swell is a clot until proved otherwise.

FAST.clue: Face, arm, speech, and time: the screen for stroke, and the clock starts at last known well
FAST.rationale: A positive FAST screen is an emergency activation, not a wait for the next set of vitals. Nothing is given by mouth until a swallow screen is done, and a CT is done before any thrombolytic.

BLEED.clue: What a CT must exclude before a thrombolytic is given for stroke, because a hemorrhagic stroke would be made worse
BLEED.rationale: Ischemic stroke may be eligible for alteplase if timing and exclusions are met. Hemorrhagic stroke is managed for pressure and blood pressure, not with anticoagulants or thrombolytics.

SWALLOW.clue: Screen that must be passed before a stroke patient gets any oral intake, including pills
SWALLOW.rationale: Aspiration pneumonia is a leading killer after stroke. Thickened liquids and a chin tuck are used only after a therapist confirms they help that patient.

BROCA.clue: Expressive aphasia: the patient understands and knows what to say but cannot get the words out
BROCA.rationale: Broca aphasia is a frontal-lobe injury. Give time, accept gestures, and do not finish every sentence or pretend not to understand the frustration.

HEMIPARESIS.clue: Weakness on one side after stroke; dress that side first, and transfer toward the stronger side
HEMIPARESIS.rationale: The nurse stands on the weak side to support the patient while the patient pivots on the strong leg. Neglect of one side requires cues to scan that side during meals and walking.

MYASTHENIA.clue: Weakness that worsens with use; give the cholinesterase inhibitor on time, and keep suction ready because of aspiration
MYASTHENIA.rationale: A myasthenic crisis is too little medication, often triggered by infection, while a cholinergic crisis is too much medication and is treated with atropine. Both can stop breathing.

GUILLAIN.clue: Ascending paralysis after an infection, often Campylobacter; the emergency is respiratory failure, treated with IVIG or plasma exchange
GUILLAIN.rationale: Guillain-Barre syndrome is monitored with vital capacity, not just oxygen saturation, because ventilation can fail while saturation still looks acceptable. Autonomic swings in heart rate and blood pressure are common.

PARKINSON.clue: Disease of resting tremor, rigidity, slow movement, and fall risk; do not stop levodopa abruptly
PARKINSON.rationale: Parkinson disease also impairs swallowing. Give levodopa on time, watch orthostatic blood pressure, and keep protein-heavy meals from competing with absorption if the prescriber has so advised.

LEVODOPA.clue: Parkinson drug that competes with protein for absorption; stopping it suddenly can mimic neuroleptic malignant syndrome
LEVODOPA.rationale: Levodopa causes nausea, orthostatic hypotension, and dyskinesias at higher doses. Carbidopa is combined with it so more drug reaches the brain and nausea is less.

VALPROATE.clue: Anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer that is teratogenic, hepatotoxic, and can drop platelets
VALPROATE.rationale: Valproate causes neural-tube defects, so pregnancy prevention is required. Report abdominal pain, because pancreatitis is another serious effect, and do not stop it abruptly.

PERRLA.clue: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation; a new unilateral dilated pupil is an emergency
PERRLA.rationale: PERRLA is part of every neuro check. Pinpoint pupils suggest opioids or a pontine lesion, and fixed dilated pupils suggest severe hypoxia or herniation.

HERNIATION.clue: Brain tissue forced downward by pressure; a unilateral dilated pupil, posturing, and a widening pulse pressure are late signs
HERNIATION.rationale: Herniation is prevented by treating intracranial pressure early: head up about 30 degrees, neck midline, no clustering of care, and no hypotonic fluids. Mannitol or hypertonic saline may be ordered.

DECEREBRATE.clue: Rigid extension posturing, which is worse than flexion posturing and points to the brainstem
DECEREBRATE.rationale: Decerebrate posturing with a falling Glasgow score means the airway and intracranial pressure are immediate priorities. Note the time and the stimulus that provoked it.

STATUS.clue: Seizure lasting more than about 5 minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery; this is an emergency treated with a benzodiazepine and airway support
STATUS.rationale: Status epilepticus is no longer defined as 30 minutes. Check glucose, give intravenous lorazepam, and follow with a longer-acting anticonvulsant so seizures do not recur.

MOUTH.clue: Never place an object or a finger here during a seizure; turn the person on the side afterward and suction if secretions pool
MOUTH.rationale: Forcing the jaw causes injury and does not prevent tongue swallowing, which is a myth. Time the seizure, loosen tight clothing, and do not restrain the limbs.

AUTONOMIC.clue: Crisis above a T6 spinal injury with pounding headache and high blood pressure; sit the patient up and remove the trigger
AUTONOMIC.rationale: Autonomic dysreflexia is usually a full bladder, stool impaction, or tight clothing. Sitting upright lowers the pressure at once, and an untreated episode can cause a stroke.

PYLORI.clue: Bacterium that causes most peptic ulcers; finish the antibiotics plus acid suppression, and confirm eradication when ordered
PYLORI.rationale: Treatment fails if the antibiotic course is shortened. Patients also stop NSAIDs and smoking, and sudden severe pain can mean perforation.

PERFORATION.clue: A hole in a hollow organ causing sudden severe pain and a rigid abdomen; keep the patient NPO and call surgery
PERFORATION.rationale: Perforation can follow an ulcer, diverticulitis, or appendicitis. Do not give laxatives or a bedside enema, and watch for shock.

RLQ.clue: Quadrant pain at McBurney point that suggests appendicitis; sudden relief can mean rupture, and heat or laxatives are forbidden
RLQ.rationale: Right-lower-quadrant pain with rebound, low fever, and anorexia is appendicitis until proved otherwise. Keep the patient NPO for possible surgery.

LLQ.clue: Usual quadrant for diverticulitis pain; during the acute infection, rest the bowel and do not do a colonoscopy
LLQ.rationale: Left-lower-quadrant pain with fever suggests diverticulitis. A colonoscopy is delayed until inflammation settles because of perforation risk, and the old ban on seeds and nuts is not required.

RUQ.clue: Quadrant pain after a fatty meal that suggests gallbladder disease and may radiate to the right shoulder
RUQ.rationale: Right-upper-quadrant pain with fever and a positive Murphy sign fits cholecystitis. Jaundice and clay-colored stools mean a stone is blocking the common duct.

LIPASE.clue: Enzyme more specific for pancreatitis than amylase; the patient is kept NPO, and pain often eases when leaning forward
LIPASE.rationale: Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain radiating to the back, often from alcohol or gallstones. Watch calcium, glucose, and breathing, because hypocalcemia and lung injury occur.

MELENA.clue: Black, tarry, foul stool from digested blood, usually an upper gastrointestinal bleed
MELENA.rationale: Melena is an emergency when it is new, especially with dizziness or a low blood pressure. Upper endoscopy is typical, and iron also darkens stool but does not make it tarry and foul in the same way.

CIRRHOSIS.clue: Scarred liver with poor clotting, low albumin, varices, and a risk of confusion from ammonia
CIRRHOSIS.rationale: Cirrhosis care is sodium restriction, no alcohol, bleeding precautions, and lactulose for encephalopathy. A falling blood pressure with a tense abdomen can be bleeding or infection of ascites.

AMMONIA.clue: Toxin that rises in hepatic encephalopathy and causes confusion plus a flapping hand tremor; lactulose traps it in the gut
AMMONIA.rationale: Lactulose is titrated to a few soft stools a day, and that diarrhea is the desired effect. Gastrointestinal bleeding and infection are common triggers, and severe protein restriction is not the modern mainstay.

JAUNDICE.clue: Yellow skin and sclera from high bilirubin; in a newborn during the first 24 hours it is abnormal and suggests hemolysis
JAUNDICE.rationale: Jaundice is checked in natural light, including the sclera. Adult causes include hepatitis, obstruction, and hemolysis, and clay stools point to obstruction.

XRAY.clue: Study required to confirm a new feeding tube or central line before it is used
XRAY.rationale: Auscultation of an air bolus does not prove a feeding tube is in the stomach. A central line is also imaged so a pneumothorax or a malpositioned tip is found before infusion.

FISTULA.clue: Dialysis access in the arm; feel the thrill, hear the bruit, and never take blood pressure or a stick in that arm
FISTULA.rationale: An arteriovenous fistula takes weeks to mature and is not used early for routine labs. No tight clothing or sleeping on that arm, and absence of a thrill is reported immediately.

THRILL.clue: Palpable vibration over a patent dialysis fistula; its absence is reported before the next dialysis
THRILL.rationale: A thrill is expected and means blood is flowing. No blood pressures, venipunctures, or tourniquets go on that arm.

DIALYSIS.clue: Treatment that pulls fluid and waste; weigh before and after, and often hold antihypertensives so the patient does not crash
DIALYSIS.rationale: Hypotension and cramps during hemodialysis are treated by slowing the removal and giving fluid as ordered. A headache and restlessness can be disequilibrium from removing solute too fast.

STOMA.clue: Ostomy opening that should be pink or red and moist; dusky, purple, or black means ischemia and is an emergency
STOMA.rationale: A new stoma is edematous, and a little bleeding with cleaning is expected. Report separation from the skin, or a marked increase in output that dehydrates the patient.

ILEOSTOMY.clue: Ostomy of the small bowel with liquid output and a high risk of dehydration; it is not irrigated
ILEOSTOMY.rationale: Ileostomy effluent is rich in enzymes and destroys skin, so the wafer must fit closely. Empty the pouch when it is about a third full, and increase fluids and electrolytes in hot weather.

DUMPING.clue: Sweating, tachycardia, and diarrhea soon after eating in a patient with gastric surgery; lie down after meals and do not drink with them
DUMPING.rationale: Dumping syndrome is limited by small, dry, high-protein, low-simple-sugar meals. Fluids are taken between meals, not with them.

CAUTI.clue: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection, prevented by sterile insertion, a bag below the bladder, and removal as soon as possible
CAUTI.rationale: CAUTI prevention is a daily question: does this catheter still need to be there? Irrigating a catheter to make it drain is not a substitute for fixing a kink or removing it.

QUICKENING.clue: First fetal movements felt by the mother, usually around 16 to 20 weeks, later in a first pregnancy
QUICKENING.rationale: Quickening is a milestone, not a complete well-being test. A clear decrease in movement later in pregnancy is evaluated the same day.

GTPAL.clue: Obstetric history code for pregnancies, term births, preterm births, abortions, and living children
GTPAL.rationale: GTPAL counts a current pregnancy in gravida. Twins delivered at term are one para event, not two, because parity counts pregnancies that reached viability, not the number of babies.

FOLIC.clue: Vitamin started before conception to lower neural-tube defect risk, commonly 400 micrograms a day
FOLIC.rationale: Folic acid must be present when the neural tube closes, often before the first missed period. A higher dose is used when a prior pregnancy had a neural-tube defect.

GDM.clue: Diabetes first recognized in pregnancy, screened around 24 to 28 weeks; the newborn is at risk for low blood sugar
GDM.rationale: Gestational diabetes is managed with diet and, when needed, insulin, which does not cross the placenta. Macrosomia raises the risk of shoulder dystocia.

PROTEINURIA.clue: Protein in the urine that, with new hypertension after 20 weeks, supports preeclampsia; severe features can be present even when protein is absent
PROTEINURIA.rationale: Headache, visual changes, epigastric pain, low platelets, and rising creatinine are severe features. Magnesium prevents seizures, and delivery is the cure.

REFLEX.clue: Deep-tendon response that disappears early in magnesium toxicity; the drug is then held
REFLEX.rationale: Magnesium for preeclampsia is held for absent reflexes, respirations often below 12 per minute, or urine output under about 30 mL per hour. Calcium gluconate is the antidote.

TERBUTALINE.clue: Beta-agonist that slows preterm contractions; hold it if the mother's heart rate is above about 120, and watch for pulmonary edema
TERBUTALINE.rationale: Terbutaline causes hyperglycemia, low potassium, and a racing heart. It is not continued if chest pain or fluid in the lungs appears.

PREVIA.clue: Placenta covering the cervix, causing painless bright-red bleeding; no vaginal exams
PREVIA.rationale: Placenta previa is confirmed by ultrasound, and delivery is often by cesarean. Digital examination can cause catastrophic bleeding.

ABRUPTION.clue: Placenta separating early, with painful dark bleeding and a rigid uterus; the bleed can be hidden
ABRUPTION.rationale: Abruption is an emergency for mother and fetus, and the risk rises with hypertension, trauma, and cocaine. Prepare for delivery and for blood replacement.

PROLAPSE.clue: Umbilical cord slipping ahead of the baby; lift the presenting part with a gloved hand and do not take the hand away
PROLAPSE.rationale: Cord prolapse uses knee-chest or Trendelenburg position, oxygen, and emergency cesarean. Do not push the cord back in, and stop oxytocin.

KNEECHEST.clue: Position that uses gravity to take the baby's weight off a prolapsed cord
KNEECHEST.rationale: Knee-chest or a steep Trendelenburg position is used while a hand lifts the presenting part. Oxygen is given and the operating room is called.

VEALCHOP.clue: Memory aid: variable decelerations mean cord, early mean head, accelerations are reassuring, and late mean placental insufficiency
VEALCHOP.rationale: Variable decelerations are treated by repositioning to relieve cord pressure. Late decelerations get position change, oxygen, fluids, and oxytocin stopped.

LATE.clue: Decelerations that begin after the contraction starts and mean uteroplacental insufficiency; turn, give oxygen and fluids, and stop oxytocin
LATE.rationale: Late decelerations are a nonreassuring pattern. Left side, oxygen, an intravenous fluid bolus, and stopping the uterotonic come before waiting for the next tracing.

VARIABLE.clue: Abrupt decelerations from cord compression; reposition the mother, and an amnioinfusion may be ordered
VARIABLE.rationale: Variable decelerations look like V shapes and change with position. Prolapse is considered if they are sudden and severe after membrane rupture.

MCROBERTS.clue: Maneuver that flexes the mother's thighs onto her abdomen to free a stuck shoulder
MCROBERTS.rationale: McRoberts maneuver plus suprapubic pressure is the first response to shoulder dystocia. Fundal pressure is not used, because it wedges the shoulder harder.

SUPRAPUBIC.clue: Pressure just above the pubic bone used to dislodge a stuck anterior shoulder; fundal pressure is the wrong place
SUPRAPUBIC.rationale: Suprapubic pressure is directed to rotate the shoulder under the pubic bone. Fundal pressure worsens the impaction and is not part of shoulder-dystocia relief.

ATONY.clue: Failure of the uterus to contract, the most common cause of postpartum hemorrhage; the fundus is boggy
ATONY.rationale: Uterine atony is treated with fundal massage, an empty bladder, and uterotonics such as oxytocin. It is more likely after a long labor, multiple gestation, or magnesium.

PPH.clue: Postpartum hemorrhage, a leading cause of maternal death; massage a boggy fundus, call for help, and start the hemorrhage protocol
PPH.rationale: Soaking a pad in about 15 minutes, or more than one pad an hour, with clots or a soft uterus, is excessive. Causes include atony, laceration, retained tissue, and hematoma.

REEDA.clue: Perineal assessment: redness, edema, ecchymosis, discharge, and approximation of the edges
REEDA.rationale: REEDA is used after an episiotomy or laceration. Ice is used in the first day, then warmth such as a sitz bath, and separation or pus is reported.

MASTITIS.clue: Breast infection with a flu-like fever and a wedge of red, painful breast; keep emptying the breast, and start antibiotics
MASTITIS.rationale: Mastitis is not a reason to stop breastfeeding. Stasis from a missed feed is a common trigger, and an abscess is suspected if a mass does not improve.

RHNEGATIVE.clue: Mother who, if unsensitized, receives Rho(D) immune globulin at 28 weeks and again within 72 hours after an Rh-positive birth
RHNEGATIVE.rationale: Immune globulin is also given after miscarriage, trauma, amniocentesis, or bleeding. It does not help a mother who is already sensitized, which is why the antibody screen is checked.

ECTOPIC.clue: Pregnancy outside the uterus, usually in a tube; one-sided pain, bleeding, and shoulder pain with dizziness mean rupture
ECTOPIC.rationale: A ruptured ectopic pregnancy is hemorrhagic shock. Methotrexate is only for a stable, unruptured ectopic that meets criteria; shoulder pain and a falling blood pressure mean surgery.

HERPES.clue: Active genital lesions at the start of labor are a reason for cesarean birth so the newborn does not pass through them
HERPES.rationale: Herpes is suppressed with acyclovir in late pregnancy when prescribed. If no lesions are present at labor, vaginal birth is not automatically ruled out.

CESAREAN.clue: Birth route used for active genital herpes lesions, placenta previa, cord prolapse, and a transverse lie
CESAREAN.rationale: A prior low-transverse cesarean does not always require another; a classical uterine scar usually does. Recovery includes incision care, early walking, and the same fundal and lochia checks.

PSYCHOSIS.clue: Postpartum emergency with hallucinations or delusions and a risk of harm to the infant; do not leave the mother alone with the baby
PSYCHOSIS.rationale: Postpartum psychosis is not the baby blues. It needs immediate psychiatric treatment, while the blues are transient mood swings in the first two weeks in a mother who can still care for the infant.

PPV.clue: Positive-pressure breaths, the key step when a newborn is not breathing or the heart rate stays under 100 after drying and stimulation
PPV.rationale: Most newborns respond to drying and stimulation. If the heart rate remains under 60 despite effective ventilation, chest compressions are added at a 3-to-1 ratio with oxygen.

BULB.clue: Suction device used on a newborn's mouth first, then the nose, so a gasp does not inhale secretions
BULB.rationale: Mouth-before-nose suction is remembered as M before N. Deep, vigorous suctioning is avoided because it causes bradycardia, and routine suction of a vigorous infant is not needed.

VITAMINK.clue: Injection given in the newborn's thigh soon after birth to prevent bleeding, because the gut is sterile and cannot yet make it
VITAMINK.rationale: Vitamin K, phytonadione, is intramuscular in the vastus lateralis, not a cord treatment. Refusal is documented after teaching about hemorrhagic disease.

PKU.clue: Newborn screen for phenylketonuria; the infant needs a special low-phenylalanine formula to prevent intellectual disability
PKU.rationale: PKU testing is done after feeding has started so metabolites are present, and abnormal results are followed quickly. Ordinary formula or milk is not used.

COLDSTRESS.clue: Newborn hypothermia that burns glucose and oxygen and can cause respiratory distress and low blood sugar
COLDSTRESS.rationale: Newborns do not shiver well and use brown fat instead. Dry them, put on a hat, and use skin-to-skin or a radiant warmer so cold stress does not start a downward spiral.

FONTANEL.clue: Soft spot that is sunken in dehydration and bulging at rest when pressure is high; the anterior one closes around 12 to 18 months
FONTANEL.rationale: The posterior fontanel closes by about 2 to 3 months. Bulging while crying can be normal; bulging at rest, with vomiting or a high-pitched cry, is not.

HONEY.clue: Food withheld until 12 months because it can cause infant botulism
HONEY.rationale: Honey, including in baked goods and on a pacifier, is unsafe for infants. Botulism causes a weak cry, constipation, and descending paralysis that can stop breathing.

CARSEAT.clue: Rear-facing seat in the back, used from the first ride home, for as long as the seat's limits allow
CARSEAT.rationale: Harnesses are snug, at or below the shoulders when rear-facing, and thick coats are not worn under the straps. The front seat with an airbag is never used for an infant.

WILMS.clue: Childhood kidney tumor; do not palpate the abdomen, because handling can rupture it and spread it
WILMS.rationale: Wilms tumor may present as a flank mass and sometimes hypertension. A sign is posted on the bed that the abdomen is not to be palpated.

KAWASAKI.clue: At least 5 days of fever plus several signs such as rash, red eyes, strawberry tongue, or swollen hands; treat with immune globulin and aspirin
KAWASAKI.rationale: Kawasaki disease needs prolonged fever plus several classic mucocutaneous signs, and it can inflame the coronary arteries. Aspirin is used here despite the usual ban in children, and echocardiograms follow the vessels.

REYE.clue: Liver failure and encephalopathy in a child given aspirin during a viral illness such as influenza or chickenpox
REYE.rationale: Reye syndrome is why aspirin is not used for routine pediatric fever. Exceptions such as Kawasaki disease are specific prescriber decisions, not home use.

PROJECTILE.clue: Forceful nonbilious vomiting in a young infant that suggests pyloric stenosis, especially if the infant is hungry afterward
PROJECTILE.rationale: Pyloric stenosis causes an olive-shaped mass and metabolic alkalosis from acid loss. Electrolytes are corrected before surgical repair.

HYPOSPADIAS.clue: Urethral opening on the underside of the penis; circumcision is delayed because the foreskin is used in the repair
HYPOSPADIAS.rationale: Hypospadias is documented and the infant still voids, but the foreskin is left intact. Parents are told why the usual newborn circumcision is postponed.

PINNA.clue: Outer ear pulled down and back for drops in a child under 3 years, and up and back in older children and adults
PINNA.rationale: Warm ear drops so they do not cause dizziness, and keep the child on the side briefly afterward. Cold drops against the eardrum cause pain and a vagal response.

SHAKEN.clue: Abusive head trauma from shaking an infant, causing retinal hemorrhages and subdural bleeding, often with no outer bruise
SHAKEN.rationale: Teach caregivers to put the baby down and walk away when crying is unbearable. Vomiting, irritability, seizures, and a bulging fontanel after shaking are an emergency.

MANDATORY.clue: The nurse's duty to report suspected child or elder abuse; certainty is not required, and good-faith reports are protected
MANDATORY.rationale: Mandatory reporting is to the appropriate agency, with objective documentation. Do not investigate like a detective or warn the suspected abuser in a way that increases danger.

COARCTATION.clue: Narrowed aorta with stronger pulses and higher blood pressure in the arms than in the legs
COARCTATION.rationale: Coarctation is suspected when femoral pulses are weak in an infant. Older children may have nosebleeds, leg cramps, and rib notching, and the defect is repaired to prevent hypertension and heart failure.

ALPROSTADIL.clue: Prostaglandin infusion that keeps the ductus arteriosus open in duct-dependent congenital heart disease; apnea is a key risk
ALPROSTADIL.rationale: Alprostadil is the opposite of indomethacin, which is used to close a patent ductus in a preterm infant. The infant on alprostadil is monitored for apnea and hypotension.

SHORTENED.clue: Appearance of a leg with a hip fracture, which is also externally rotated
SHORTENED.rationale: A shortened, externally rotated leg is a hip fracture until proved otherwise. Neurovascular checks are repeated, and Buck traction may be used before surgery.

COMPARTMENT.clue: Syndrome of pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, and later pulselessness; loosen the cast and do not elevate or ice
COMPARTMENT.rationale: Compartment syndrome is a fasciotomy emergency. The first sign is severe pain, not a lost pulse, and elevation or ice reduces the remaining blood flow.

PHANTOM.clue: Pain felt in a limb that has been amputated; it is real and is treated with analgesics
PHANTOM.rationale: Phantom limb pain is not imaginary and is not the same as incisional pain, though both are treated. Do not tell the patient the limb is gone so the pain cannot exist.

ABDUCTION.clue: Pillow position after a posterior hip replacement that keeps the legs apart so the hip does not dislocate
ABDUCTION.rationale: Posterior approach precautions are no adduction past midline, no flexion past 90 degrees, and no internal rotation. The patient does not cross the legs or bend to tie shoes.

ALENDRONATE.clue: Bisphosphonate taken in the morning with a full glass of water, then the patient stays upright for 30 minutes and eats nothing else yet
ALENDRONATE.rationale: Alendronate prevents esophageal burns only if the patient does not lie down. Report jaw pain, and do not take it with coffee, juice, or other pills.

DEHISCENCE.clue: Separation of a wound edge; cover it with a sterile moist dressing, have the patient flex the knees slightly, and call the surgeon
DEHISCENCE.rationale: Dehiscence often follows a pop after coughing in an obese or malnourished patient. If organs protrude, do not push them back, keep the patient NPO, and stay at the bedside.

EVISCERATE.clue: Organs protruding through a separated wound; cover them with sterile saline gauze, do not push them back, and keep the knees bent
EVISCERATE.rationale: Evisceration is a surgical emergency. Low Fowler position with knees flexed reduces strain, and the patient is kept NPO for the operating room.

DANTROLENE.clue: Antidote for malignant hyperthermia, a crisis of high carbon dioxide, rigidity, and then high fever triggered by certain anesthetics
DANTROLENE.rationale: Dantrolene is given as soon as malignant hyperthermia is suspected, the triggering gas is stopped, and 100 percent oxygen is given. Fever is late; a rising end-tidal carbon dioxide is early.

STERILE.clue: Technique in which a 1-inch border, anything below the waist, and a wet field are considered contaminated
STERILE.rationale: Sterile gloves are used for invasive procedures such as a Foley insertion. Do not turn your back on the field, and do not reach over it.

TIMEOUT.clue: Pause immediately before incision to confirm the right patient, procedure, and site, plus allergies and antibiotics
TIMEOUT.rationale: Any team member can stop a time-out. The site marking is checked with the consent, and the procedure does not start until the pause is complete.

INFORMED.clue: Consent in which the provider explains risks, benefits, and alternatives, and the nurse verifies understanding and witnesses the signature
INFORMED.rationale: The nurse does not obtain consent by explaining the surgery in the provider's place. A sedated or confused patient cannot sign, and the nurse does not witness a signature the patient does not understand.

PARKLAND.clue: Burn fluid formula using lactated Ringer: 4 mL times weight in kilograms times percent burned, with half given in the first 8 hours from the time of injury
PARKLAND.rationale: The Parkland clock starts at the burn, not at arrival, so delayed care means a faster initial rate. Urine output, about 0.5 mL/kg per hour in adults, shows whether the volume is enough.

LATEX.clue: Allergy more common after many surgeries and in spina bifida, and linked to banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut
LATEX.rationale: A latex-allergic patient is first on the schedule in a latex-reduced room, with latex-free gloves and catheters. Balloons and powdered gloves do not enter.

ELECTRICAL.clue: Burn that can have a small skin wound and huge internal damage; monitor the heart and the urine for muscle pigment
ELECTRICAL.rationale: Electrical injury causes dysrhythmias and rhabdomyolysis. Cervical spine precautions are used if the patient fell, and urine output targets are higher to flush myoglobin.

THERMAL.clue: Heat burn; cool with water, not ice, remove jewelry, and cover with a clean dry sheet
THERMAL.rationale: Ice worsens thermal injury by constricting vessels. Do not apply butter or ointments to a major burn, and treat airway smoke exposure first.

UAP.clue: Assistive personnel who may take routine vital signs on a stable patient, help with hygiene and walking, and record intake and output, but do not assess or teach
UAP.rationale: Unlicensed assistive personnel do not give medications, perform sterile procedures, or take a newly unstable patient. The nurse follows up on any abnormal value they report.

DELEGATION.clue: Transfer of a task using the right task, circumstance, person, direction, and supervision; assessment, teaching, and evaluation stay with the RN
DELEGATION.rationale: The nurse who delegates remains accountable for the outcome and must say what to report back and when.

ASSESSMENT.clue: The initial and ongoing comprehensive judgment that the RN does not delegate
ASSESSMENT.rationale: Collecting a vital sign can be delegated; interpreting a new change and examining the patient cannot. If the status changes, the RN takes the patient back.

RACE.clue: Fire response order: rescue the patient, activate the alarm, contain the fire, then extinguish or evacuate
RACE.rationale: Rescue comes before the extinguisher. Oxygen is shut off if it can be done safely, doors are closed to contain smoke, and ambulatory patients are moved past the fire doors.

PASS.clue: Extinguisher steps: pull the pin, aim at the base, squeeze, and sweep
PASS.rationale: Aim at the base of the fire, not the flames. PASS is used only after RACE has started and if the fire is small and the exit is at your back.

PRN.clue: An as-needed order, which is never acceptable as the only order for a restraint
PRN.rationale: Restraint orders are time-limited and based on a current assessment, not written 'PRN restraint.' Pain medicine and laxatives can be PRN; tying a patient cannot.

INCIDENT.clue: Internal safety report after an error or a near miss; it is not mentioned in the medical record and does not replace factual charting
INCIDENT.rationale: The chart states what happened and what was done for the patient. It does not say that an incident report was filed, and the report is not copied into the chart.

TEACHBACK.clue: Asking the patient to explain or demonstrate, which confirms understanding better than a nod or a yes
TEACHBACK.rationale: Teach-back is 'show me how you will take this,' not 'do you understand?' Reteach in a different way if the explanation is wrong, and do it when pain and anxiety are controlled.

INTERPRETER.clue: Qualified language professional required for consent and teaching; do not use a child or an untrained family member
INTERPRETER.rationale: Speak to the patient, not to the interpreter, and use teach-back. A bilingual staff member is used only if that person is an approved interpreter.

DOXORUBICIN.clue: Chemotherapy that can cause heart failure as the lifetime dose adds up, and that turns urine red, which is expected and not blood
DOXORUBICIN.rationale: Doxorubicin is a vesicant, so extravasation is treated immediately and the infusion is not flushed blindly. Ejection fraction is checked, and the cumulative dose is tracked.

VINCRISTINE.clue: Chemotherapy that causes nerve damage and severe constipation and is fatal if given into the spinal fluid
VINCRISTINE.rationale: Vincristine is intravenous only and is fatal if given into the spinal fluid. Start a bowel regimen early, report numbness, and remember that it causes little marrow suppression.

NADIR.clue: Lowest blood counts after chemotherapy, often 7 to 14 days later, when infection and bleeding risk peak
NADIR.rationale: The nadir is when neutropenic precautions and bleeding precautions are strictest. A fever at nadir is an emergency, not a symptom to mention at the next visit.

TLS.clue: Tumor lysis syndrome: after chemotherapy, uric acid, potassium, and phosphate rise and calcium falls; hydrate and monitor the heart
TLS.rationale: Tumor lysis can cause fatal arrhythmias from hyperkalemia. Allopurinol or a similar drug plus fluids limit uric acid, and the patient is on a cardiac monitor.

IRON.clue: Mineral taken with vitamin C, not with milk or antacids; liquid doses use a straw so teeth do not stain, and stools turn dark
IRON.rationale: Iron is best on an empty stomach if it is tolerated, and constipation is expected. It does not fix anemia from B12 deficiency, and children can be fatally poisoned by adult tablets.

COBALAMIN.clue: Vitamin B12, missing in pernicious anemia because intrinsic factor is absent; nerve damage can become permanent if replacement is delayed
COBALAMIN.rationale: B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia plus paresthesias and ataxia. Folate alone can fix the anemia and hide the deficiency while the nerves keep dying.

FOLATE.clue: Vitamin whose deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia without the nerve damage of B12 deficiency, and whose use before conception lowers neural-tube defect risk
FOLATE.rationale: Folate is started before pregnancy, commonly 400 micrograms daily, because the neural tube closes very early. Alcohol use and methotrexate interfere with folate.

SICKLING.clue: Red cells crescent under low oxygen, dehydration, or cold; prevention is fluids, warmth, and infection control
SICKLING.rationale: Sickle cell crisis pain is treated with opioids other than meperidine, plus fluids and oxygen if saturation is low. Fever is an emergency because the spleen does not clear encapsulated bacteria.

FACTOR.clue: Replacement that stops bleeding in hemophilia; do not give aspirin or intramuscular injections
FACTOR.rationale: Hemophilia A lacks factor VIII and hemophilia B lacks factor IX. Joint bleeding is rested, iced, compressed, and elevated, and the missing factor is given promptly.

EPOETIN.clue: Injection that stimulates red-cell production in chronic kidney disease; it can raise blood pressure and clot risk, and the vial is not shaken
EPOETIN.rationale: Epoetin is not titrated to a normal hemoglobin, because higher targets increase stroke and thrombosis. Check blood pressure before the dose.

REJECTION.clue: Fever, graft tenderness, and rising creatinine after a kidney transplant; immunosuppressants are lifelong and doses are not skipped
REJECTION.rationale: Rejection is reported the same day. The tradeoff of tacrolimus and similar drugs is infection and nephrotoxicity, and grapefruit is avoided.

JACKSON.clue: Closed drain whose bulb is compressed to restore suction; a sudden increase or foul odor is reported
JACKSON.rationale: A Jackson-Pratt drain is emptied and measured, and the bulb is recollapsed. It is not stripped routinely, and it is not advanced or removed without an order.

CONTRAST.clue: Iodinated dye that can injure kidneys; hold metformin around the study, hydrate, and ask about prior dye reactions rather than about shellfish
CONTRAST.rationale: A shellfish allergy does not predict contrast reaction. Metformin is held because of lactic acidosis risk if the kidneys are injured, and creatinine is checked.

VESICANT.clue: Chemotherapy that blisters tissue if it extravasates; stop the infusion for burning, and do not flush the line blindly
VESICANT.rationale: A vesicant protocol usually leaves the catheter in place so the drug can be aspirated and an antidote given. Apply the ordered compress, not a random heat or ice pack.

ONDANSETRON.clue: Antiemetic given before chemotherapy, not after vomiting is severe; it prolongs the QT interval and causes headache
ONDANSETRON.rationale: Ondansetron is a serotonin blocker and can constipate. It is less useful for nausea from vestibular causes or from a full bowel obstruction.

BLEOMYCIN.clue: Chemotherapy that scars the lungs; high oxygen concentrations are avoided when possible because they worsen the injury
BLEOMYCIN.rationale: Bleomycin toxicity shows as cough, dyspnea, and a falling diffusion capacity. Pulmonary function is followed, and fever during infusion can occur.

CEPHALIC.clue: Head-down fetal presentation, the favorable position for a vaginal birth
CEPHALIC.rationale: A flexed head-down presentation is the most favorable. Breech and transverse lies raise the risk of cord prolapse and usually need a cesarean plan.

SHAVER.clue: Use an electric one rather than a blade when platelets are low or the patient is anticoagulated
SHAVER.rationale: Bleeding precautions also include a soft toothbrush, no intramuscular injections, no rectal temperatures, and prolonged pressure on puncture sites.

TAMPON.clue: Item that, if left in too long, can cause sudden fever, rash, and low blood pressure; a diaphragm left in too long can do the same
TAMPON.rationale: Toxic shock is treated as sepsis: remove the device, give fluids and antibiotics, and teach patients to change tampons every few hours.

RSV.clue: Virus that causes bronchiolitis in infants; use contact precautions, suction, and oxygen, not routine antibiotics
RSV.rationale: Respiratory syncytial virus is most dangerous in young infants. Palivizumab can prevent severe disease in high-risk infants and is not a treatment for an active infection.

HOB.clue: Head of the bed, raised at least 30 degrees during tube feeding and for about an hour afterward to prevent aspiration
HOB.rationale: HOB elevation is also the position for dyspnea and for intracranial-pressure control around 30 degrees. Supine feeding is an aspiration setup.

NST.clue: Abbreviation for the fetal nonstress test; reactive means two accelerations in 20 minutes
NST.rationale: The NST uses an external monitor and does not use contractions. Vibroacoustic stimulation may be used to wake a sleeping fetus before calling the test nonreactive.

AKI.clue: Acute kidney injury, sorted as poor perfusion, kidney damage, or obstruction; potassium and fluid are restricted when urine output is very low
AKI.rationale: Prerenal injury from dehydration can reverse with careful fluids. Intrarenal injury such as acute tubular necrosis and postrenal obstruction need different treatment, and contrast and NSAIDs are common toxins.

NEC.clue: Necrotizing enterocolitis of preterm infants: feeding intolerance, a distended belly, and bloody stool; stop feeds
NEC.rationale: NEC is a bowel emergency with a risk of perforation. The infant is made NPO, an abdominal film is done, and antibiotics and surgical consultation follow.

TPN.clue: Intravenous nutrition through a central line; if the bag runs out, hang a dextrose infusion so blood sugar does not crash
TPN.rationale: Total parenteral nutrition is a high infection risk and needs strict asepsis and glucose checks. Lipids are given on their own schedule, and the line is not used casually for blood draws and incompatible drugs.

DIC.clue: Consumptive clotting that uses up factors and platelets, so the patient both clots and bleeds; it complicates sepsis, abruption, and trauma
DIC.rationale: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is treated by fixing the cause, such as delivering the placenta or treating sepsis, and by replacing blood products. Heparin is sometimes used but is not the first nursing action.
